brief.summary: A qualitative-coding workbench for computational social science labs that hands an AI model a codebook and a corpus of online-community posts to code, then lets researchers check its work against human-coded samples before accepting any of it into the dataset.
brief.user: Priya Ramaswamy, a fourth-year PhD student in a university lab that studies mutual-aid communities online. brief.moment: Yesterday afternoon Priya gave the model a job: apply codebook v3 to 3,800 posts collected from four mutual-aid forums between 2021 and 2024. It has finished 1,240. Comparing against the 300 posts she and a second coder labeled by hand, agreement is strong on 'offer of help' (kappa 0.86) but weak on 'request for help' (0.61), and the model keeps labeling venting posts that end in a question as requests. brief.data: Corpus: 3,800 posts from r-style forums 'MutualAidPDX', 'RentReliefNet', 'NeighborsHelpingNeighbors' and 'GigWorkerCommons', each with post ID, date, anonymized author hash and text (median 140 words). Codebook v3: 9 codes (request for help, offer of help, venting, logistics, gratitude, rule enforcement, resource sharing, off-topic, unclear), each with a definition, inclusion and exclusion rules and 2–4 examples, and a change log back to v1. Job state: 1,240 of 3,800 coded, started Nov 15 at 2:12 pm, model 'claude-research-2026-09', estimated cost so far $18.40. Each AI label carries the code, a confidence of 0–1, the quoted sentence it relied on, a one-line rationale, and the codebook version used. Gold sample: 300 posts double-coded by Priya and Marcus Bell; 41 disagreements between the model and the gold labels, 23 of them on 'request for help'. Lab policy note from the PI, Dr. Elena Voss: no AI labels go into analysis unless agreement on every code is at least 0.75.

prompt:
I need the front end for Threadcoder. A qualitative-coding workbench for computational social science labs that hands an AI model a codebook and a corpus of online-community posts to code, then lets researchers check its work against human-coded samples before accepting any of it into the dataset.

Who's using it: Priya Ramaswamy, a fourth-year PhD student in a university lab that studies mutual-aid communities online. She wrote the lab's codebook, has hand-coded hundreds of posts herself, and will defend these labels in her dissertation and in a paper under review, so she needs to know where every label came from.

What they're doing right now: Yesterday afternoon Priya gave the model a job: apply codebook v3 to 3,800 posts collected from four mutual-aid forums between 2021 and 2024. It has finished 1,240. Comparing against the 300 posts she and a second coder labeled by hand, agreement is strong on 'offer of help' (kappa 0.86) but weak on 'request for help' (0.61), and the model keeps labeling venting posts that end in a question as requests. She needs to read the disagreements, tighten the definition of 'request for help' with two new boundary examples, pause the run and restart it from the point of the change, and decide whether the first 1,240 labels are kept, re-run, or thrown out.

What's in the system at this point: Corpus: 3,800 posts from r-style forums 'MutualAidPDX', 'RentReliefNet', 'NeighborsHelpingNeighbors' and 'GigWorkerCommons', each with post ID, date, anonymized author hash and text (median 140 words). Codebook v3: 9 codes (request for help, offer of help, venting, logistics, gratitude, rule enforcement, resource sharing, off-topic, unclear), each with a definition, inclusion and exclusion rules and 2–4 examples, and a change log back to v1. Job state: 1,240 of 3,800 coded, started Nov 15 at 2:12 pm, model 'claude-research-2026-09', estimated cost so far $18.40. Each AI label carries the code, a confidence of 0–1, the quoted sentence it relied on, a one-line rationale, and the codebook version used. Gold sample: 300 posts double-coded by Priya and Marcus Bell; 41 disagreements between the model and the gold labels, 23 of them on 'request for help'. Lab policy note from the PI, Dr. Elena Voss: no AI labels go into analysis unless agreement on every code is at least 0.75.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
